Sound design — treating the server's pending-prompt list as the source of truth at bootstrap (with a comment explaining *why*: process-local state orphaned by restarts) plus a verify-then-dismiss path on settlement failure covers both halves of the stale-prompt problem. I verified the risky bits hold together: `question.asked` inserts via the same binary-search helper the new `dismiss()` uses (`packages/tui/src/context/sync.tsx:411-444`), so the id-sorted invariant required by `search()` survives mixing event-fed and hydrated entries; and `reply()` resolving as an `{error}` object rather than throwing matches this SDK's generated-client style, so `settle()` won't silently miss failures.

Two suggestions:

1. **Same treatment for permissions.** `permission.reply`/`reject` failing against an orphaned request leaves the identical unanswerable dialog; the hydration half now covers permissions (`packages/tui/src/context/sync.tsx:~545-551`) but there's no runtime `dismiss`-on-failure equivalent for `permission.tsx`. Either add it for symmetry or note why questions are special.

2. **Inconsistent scoping between the two list calls.** Bootstrap queries `list({ workspace })` (`sync.tsx:~546`) while `settle()` queries `list({ directory: props.directory })` (`packages/tui/src/routes/session/question.tsx:~54`). If a workspace-level list ever spans directories the TUI isn't showing, the membership check could disagree with what bootstrap hydrated. Worth aligning both on the same scope parameter (or documenting why they intentionally differ).

Test coverage is genuinely good here — hydrate/drop-on-rebootstrap and double-dismiss are exactly the cases worth pinning (`packages/tui/test/cli/cmd/tui/sync-pending-prompts.test.tsx:171-218`). Nice-to-have: one case asserting settle does *not* dismiss when the server still lists the request (transient reply failure).

Well-scoped workaround for a nasty class of leak — hooking `"aborted"` and destroying the response to force Bun's missing `"close"` is the least invasive fix available, the comment citing the upstream issue (`packages/core/src/util/http-server.ts:30-37`) is much appreciated, and the `process.versions.bun` gate keeps Node/Electron behavior byte-identical. Both production listeners are wired (`packages/cli/src/commands/handlers/serve.ts:43`, `packages/opencode/src/server/server.ts:201`), and the tests use real sockets including the negative case (`packages/core/test/util/http-server.test.ts:68-110`). Two notes:

1. **Residual leak for silent disconnects.** `"aborted"` fires on an explicit client teardown of the request, but a peer that vanishes without FIN/RST (laptop sleep, NAT drop) emits nothing, so those SSE streams still accumulate until the next `response.write()` fails. Periodic SSE heartbeats would self-heal this; otherwise worth adding one line to the doc comment acknowledging the bridge only covers the explicit-abort case, so future readers don't assume it's total.

2. **Coverage check on other servers.** `packages/stats/server/src/server.ts` also builds a `node:http` server that runs under whatever runtime hosts it — if any of its routes are long-lived/streaming, it needs `bridgeClientDisconnect` too; if everything is short-request/response, fine as-is. (The WSL sidecar uses `node:net`, so it's unaffected.)

Minor: the `writableEnded`/`destroyed` check at `http-server.ts:42` has an inherent TOCTOU window against concurrent `end()`, but destroying an ended response is harmless — no action needed.

Correct fix for a real race — the old order (publish first, settle/delete after) let a second reply slip through `pending.get()` while listeners delayed the first publish inside `events.publish`, producing double settlement and duplicate broadcasts. Claiming the entry first, restoring it only when the *publish itself* fails, is exactly right, and moving `pending.delete()` before the deferred resolution keeps list-pollers consistent with the broadcast. The `Array.from(pending)` snapshots in both cascade loops (`packages/core/src/permission.ts:~245, ~267`) are necessary now that the loop mutates mid-iteration across suspension points. The gated-listener tests are the highlight: they deterministically reproduce the interleaving and assert exactly-one event, `NotFoundError` for the loser, and an empty final list (`packages/core/test/permission.test.ts:286-319`, mirrored for questions including reject in `question.test.ts:92-128`).

Two small suggestions:

1. **The claim→publish→restore-on-error sequence is now copy-pasted four times** (`permission.ts` primary/reject-cascade/always-cascade, `question.ts` reply/reject). Extracting a `settleClaimed(id, item, event)` helper would keep the invariant in one place — this is precisely the kind of subtle ordering that drifts in future edits.

2. **Cascade failure path is untested.** Both tests gate only the *primary* publish. A companion test making the second (cascaded) publish fail would pin the recovery semantics: earlier items stay settled, the failing item is restored to `pending`, and the error propagates without corrupting the map.

Impressive amount of working code, and the ARM64 motivation is real — but I'd push back on landing this as-is into the monorepo root. Substantive points:

1. **Architecture: a parallel, divergent agent inside the official repo.** `desktop-arm64/` re-implements SSE parsing, providers, sessions, and tools that already exist in `packages/core`/`packages/desktop`, with its own toolchain (npm + `node --test`, `desktop-arm64/package.json:15-25`) while the repo standardizes on bun/bun:test. Being intentionally excluded from workspaces means CI never builds or tests any of these 26 files, so they will rot silently. Windows-ARM64 support belongs as an Electron build target of the existing `packages/desktop`; if it genuinely can't share code yet, an out-of-repo fork (the README/package description already call it "unofficial… not built by the OpenCode team", `package.json:6-9`) fits that framing better than the org's repo.

2. **Factual premise error in the README** (`desktop-arm64/README.md:11-16`): the table claims the upstream desktop app is "Tauri/Rust". This repo's desktop package is Electron (`packages/desktop/src/main/windows.ts`, `ipc.ts` use `BrowserWindow`/`ipcMain`). Since Electron already ships win32-arm64 prebuilds, the "no native path" justification needs correcting or restating against actual upstream facts.

3. **Chunk-boundary decoding bug in `runShellCommand`** (`desktop-arm64/src/core/tools.ts:~524-556`): `d.toString("utf8")` per chunk corrupts multibyte characters split across reads, and the `stdout.length < cap` check appends whole chunks so the buffer can overshoot 64KB arbitrarily. Use `node:string_decoder`'s `StringDecoder` and truncate once on the decoder output.

4. Minor: `docs/screenshot.png` committed as a repo blob — prefer linking it from the docs site or release notes.

1. **Worth documenting *why* NUL breaks a write.** If the terminal route base64-encodes payloads for OSC 52, embedded NULs are harmless there, so the failure presumably comes from a path that emits text verbatim (or from native bridge APIs that treat NUL as a terminator, C-string style). A one-line comment naming the actual breaking consumer would keep a future refactor from dropping the sanitizer as "obviously unnecessary". It also clarifies whether other control characters (e.g. lone `\x07` BEL) need similar treatment for that route.

2. **Silent mutation tradeoff:** `replaceAll("\0", "")` alters content without any signal. Fine given NULs are almost never intentional in copied text, but consider a debug-level log when characters are removed so users diagnosing odd paste output have a trail.

Otherwise good to merge.

The perf diagnosis is credible and the pieces I like most are the in-process `statUntracked` (with a ground-truth-vs-real-numstat test covering LF/CRLF/no-trailing-newline/binary — excellent, `packages/opencode/test/git/git.test.ts:737-769`) and widening the watcher's `.git` ignore exception to `refs`/`packed-refs`/`index` (`packages/core/src/filesystem/watcher.ts:119-126`) so cache invalidation has a real signal. Four concerns:

1. **Positive-only discover memo can go stale the other way** (`packages/core/src/git.ts:184-192, 205-214`). Negative results stay uncached to pick up later `git init`, but a *deleted* `.git`, removed worktree, or `GIT_DIR` relocation keeps returning the old `Repository` for the 10-minute TTL, and every subsequent git call then fails against a nonexistent dir. Consider invalidating the cached entry when a downstream command reports a missing git directory, instead of time alone.

2. **Single-flight key collisions** (`packages/opencode/src/git/index.ts:132-143`). `${cwd}\0${args.join(" ")}` conflates `["--","a b"]` with `["--","a","b"]`; use `JSON.stringify(args)`. Also `opts.env` isn't part of the key — today nothing passes a distinguishing env, but one future caller doing `GIT_DIR=…` gets another caller's output silently. Either add env to the key or refuse to share when `env !== undefined`.

3. **Degradation trigger over-fires** (`packages/opencode/src/project/vcs.ts:~415-420`). `value.length > UNTRACKED_DEGRADE_AT` counts *all* status entries, so a legitimately huge repo with thousands of *tracked* modifications gets flipped to `--untracked-files=normal` and persisted forever in `vcs-degraded.json`, degrading untracked detail for a normal repo. Gate on the untracked subset (`item.status === "added"` count) instead.

4. **Diff hygiene:** both test files appear as full-file rewrites (every line `-`/`+`) with unchanged content — looks like EOL normalization. Restoring the original line endings keeps the actually-added tests reviewable.

Otherwise solid; #3 is the one I'd require before merge.

```
level=INFO  message=file mime=application/json
```

+1 — we just had a real incident caused by exactly this gap (OpenCode 1.18.21, openrouter/google/gemini-3.7-flash, reasoning high).

While the agent was in a long tool-call loop, I typed "what are you doing right now?" twice. Both messages were written to the session (visible in opencode.db as user rows inserted mid-stream), but since there is no queue/steer/break distinction they were just appended as the next user message after the next tool result — no priority, no wrapper, no turn boundary. The model never produced a text answer; its reasoning parts literally said "I was directly addressing your question", then it kept executing its previous plan with more tool calls. It escalated past a failing pre-push review gate (tried an env-var bypass, then wrote a fake review marker) and ran git push origin main. Only a double-Esc abort killed the push ~300 ms in. Its next reasoning step then falsely claimed the push had succeeded and started a production deploy sequence.

So from the user's perspective: my questions "arrived" but were effectively ignored, because the harness gives a mid-run prompt no semantics at all — the model alone decides whether to react. Stronger models tend to answer; Gemini Flash-class models treated it as noise.

What would have prevented this:
- break as the default for a mid-run prompt (or at least a configurable default), so a new user message always ends the current step and gets answered before any further tool call;
- steer messages wrapped/marked as such (related: #16102, #21518) so the model can't mistake them for old context;
- queue not being silently dropped on abort (#5333).

Solid, well-tested protocol work overall: the lowering/replay round-trip is covered by tests, and the guardrails rejecting `tool_choice` by name and `allowed_tools` containing `local_shell` are exactly right given the API's constraints. A few concerns, mostly around wire-format fidelity:

1. **`local_shell_call_output` looks to be missing `call_id`** (`packages/ai/src/protocols/openai-responses.ts:64-68` and the mapping at `:171`). The emitted item is `{ type, id: item.call_id, output }`, but OpenAI's Responses API expects a `call_id` field on `local_shell_call_output` items. As written, replaying any shell turn would likely get a 400 from the real endpoint — the tests only validate against your own decoder, so they can't catch this. Suggest adding `call_id: Schema.String` to `OpenAIResponsesLocalShellCallOutput` and emitting `call_id: item.call_id` (keeping `id` optional/derived from the original item). Worth verifying once against the live API.

2. **`env` is required in the action decoder** (`packages/ai/src/protocols/openai-responses.ts:53`) and in the exposed tool schema (`packages/ai/src/providers/openai.ts`, `required: ["type", "command", "env"]` around line 76). If the model omits `env` (plausible — it's not semantically required to execute a command), `onLocalShellCallDone` fails the whole generation with "local_shell_call is malformed". Making `env` optional (or defaulting to `{}`) in the decoder is safer; forcing it in the tool schema also pushes models to invent environment values.

3. **Silent fallback when provider metadata is lost** (`packages/ai/src/protocols/openai-responses.ts:162-164`). If a session is resumed without `providerMetadata` (serialization round-trip, transcript hand-editing), history stays as `function_call`/`function_call_output` named `local_shell` while `tools` contains `{ type: "local_shell" }` — the API will reject that pairing with an opaque error. Consider failing fast with a clear `invalidRequest` ("local_shell call lost provider metadata; cannot replay") instead.

4. **Possibly-undefined `action`/`status`** (`:166-169`): the rebuilt `local_shell_call` can carry `undefined` fields when metadata is incomplete, which then fails `decodeBody` with a generic schema message rather than something actionable. Fine to keep, but a targeted error would help debugging.

Minor: `request.model.route.providerMetadataKey ?? "openai"` is duplicated in `localShellCalls` (`:152`) and `lowerLocalShellHistory` (`:167`) — worth hoisting into one lookup helper.

For anyone landing here from a search: there are **two different causes** behind this same `SchemaError(Missing key ...)` message, and they need different fixes. Worth checking which one you actually have before trying anything, because the fix for the second one isn't a plugin.

Look at the recorded tool input for a failed call:

| Tool input | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `{"fileContent": "...", "path": "..."}` | model used synonym keys | key normalization |
| `{}` — empty | model emitted no arguments at all | provider `limit` config |

### 1. Mis-keyed arguments

This is the case in the original report — the model sends the right values under the wrong names (`fileContent` for `content`, `path` for `filePath`). The error names the missing key but never says what the model *should* have sent, so it retries the same shape and loops.

This can be fixed from userland with no rebuild, because `tool.execute.before` runs *before* the schema decode and receives the live args object (in `session/tools.ts`, `plugin.trigger("tool.execute.before", …)` precedes `item.execute`). Renaming the key in place there makes the call succeed rather than just producing a better error.

Plugin doing that, plus reordering the `write` schema so `filePath` is declared before `content`: https://github.com/VRIL-LABS/better-write-opencode — MIT, drop one file into `~/.config/opencode/plugins/`.

### 2. Empty `{}` arguments — this one is a config issue

If the failing input is an empty object, there are no keys to rename and **no plugin can help**. The model degenerated and emitted a tool call with no arguments.

In my case this traced back to auto-compaction never running. Custom providers default to `limit.context = 0`, and `isOverflow()` in `session/overflow.ts` returns early on exactly that:

```ts
if (input.model.limit.context === 0) return false
```

So with a custom `@ai-sdk/openai-compatible` provider that doesn't declare limits, compaction never fires, context grows unbounded, and the model eventually emits argument-less tool calls. Measured over one session: tool calls succeeded at ~66k input tokens on average, and failed from ~80k all the way up to 167k. Every single failure had `input = {}` — 70 `bash`, 18 `write`.

The fix is to declare limits on the model:

```jsonc
"models": {
  "your-model": {
    "limit": {
      "context": 262144,   // the model's real window
      "input":    80000,   // compaction trigger
      "output":   32768
    }
  }
}
```

`limit.input` is the useful knob here — `usable = limit.input − reserved`, so you can declare the true context window while still compacting early enough to stay in the range where the model reliably emits well-formed tool calls.

---

Either way, none of this requires `edit: deny` / `write: deny`. Hope it saves someone the same detour.
